Ok I thought about this a bit more. It took me a while to finally understand what @dwarkesh_sp was getting at by casting the discussion into a formal economics model. We were simply talking past each other.

Fundamentally, the “intuition” Dwarkesh was pointing to is that AI research progress is produced by a combination of researcher effort and experiment compute that are imperfect substitutes. The production function of AI capability is concave (“isoquants” are convex), so using a more balanced mix is always more productive for a given budget than being stuck in a corner.

Research automation changes this in two distinct ways. First, it raises the effective quantity of the researcher input since automated researchers work much faster and continuously, so each one delivers say “50×” more researcher input per calendar week. Because of concavity, that does not translate into a 50× speedup in final research output for a fixed compute budget; Dwarkesh’s rough lower bound is still something like “5×”.

Second, and perhaps more importantly, automation also raises the productivity of the AI capability production process itself. It’s almost like there’s a technology or productivity multiplier that rises with each generation of smarter models. Once models match the best humans, every automated researcher is at the level of today’s top researchers (in his words), and the work is modular enough to be highly parallelized. (I’m not sure whether this last part is really even necessary.)

These quality and parallelism channels are each equivalent to an endogenous rise in a technology multiplier in front of the production function, which in turn raises the quality and effective quantity of researcher input into the next research production cycle. Here we get an explicit mechanism for recursive self-improvement (RSI).

This is essentially the same structure as a Paul Romer-style labor augmenting technology endogenous growth model applied to the AI research sector itself. The stock of AI capability (S) evolves according to a law of motion of the form (\dot{S} = k S^\theta), where the exponent (\theta) reflects how stronger prior capability improvements raise both effective researcher quantity and research quality.

If (\theta > 1), the feedback is superlinear and we get what he calls a “software-only singularity”: progress accelerates iteratively with AI research quantity and quality even on existing compute. If (\theta < 1) (or is eventually pulled below 1 by the fact that ideas get harder to find), we get a so called “spark” or a large but finite burst of progress that peters out. Further gains require more compute. 

Dwarkesh’s core claim is that (\theta) is likely currently big enough that automating AI research with AI models can kick off or produce at least a substantial spark, and even possibly a “software-only singularity”.

It turns out the contrasts of “50x vs 5x” or “human researchers only vs fully automated researchers” were red herrings that were inconsequential to what he was arguing. Perhaps what he said was clear enough to everyone else and I just got hung up on the wrong things. 🤦🏻‍♂️

Both the Biden and Trump administrations allowed the export of less powerful GPUs to China while reserving the most advanced chips for America. This has been a clear national security success.

Per Grok and Claude, the US-to-China AI FLOPs ratio has grown from 2.8x in 2023 to 8.8x in 2026 and is modeled to reach 14.1x in 2027. Our advantage in compute has grown dramatically and American AI labs have stayed well ahead of Chinese labs the entire time.

Chinese labs prefer these less powerful American GPUs to domestic accelerators from Huawei and others. That preference has slowed China’s hardware industry: AI chips improve through intensive use by leading labs, and the ready availability of American alternatives has limited that feedback loop for Chinese AI hardware.

Chinese labs can also access capacity in Southeast Asian clouds run by American hyperscalers. Those zones can be shut off instantly in a conflict, giving the US signficant leverage. This dependence is advantageous in every way.

A complete ban on GPU exports and Southeast Asian cloud access might be deeply damaging to long-term American national security. It would force Chinese labs onto the Huawei AI hardware ecosystem. China is not power-constrained, and Huawei is developing extremely power-hungry, large optical scale-up domains that may approach American state-of-the-art systems through brute force rather than architectural elegance and efficiency. And China has a lot of power.

Having Chinese labs optimize models for this different architecture is risky as nothing prevents China from sharing this hardware and associated models with Russia, North Korea, or Iran. We would lose any ability to cut off their AI in a conflict.

Policies now under discussion in Washington carry serious, uncertain risks. Reasonable minds can disagree, but treating this as a simple black-and-white issue does America a disservice.

If China closes the installed FLOPs gap as its domestic hardware matures rapidly as a result of increased Chinese lab usage after stricter export controls, we will know this new policy was a mistake.

If Russia, Iran, or North Korea later field comparable Chinese AI hardware systems that are used to run AI targeting models against Ukrainian or American troops, we will know stricter controls were a *terrible* mistake.

The current reality is one where China is consistently behind America thanks to the export of less powerful GPUs and we have immense leverage over China in any future conflict. We know that the current policy is working. We have no idea what the consequences of stricter controls might be.

This is why China is currently restricting imports of roughly 600,000 H200s sitting in Hong Kong warehouses. China Hawks should consider why Beijing agrees with them and why China *restricts* the sales American GPUs inside China.

The current policy has worked spectacularly. The alternative is extremely risky with unknown consequences.

If you look at my tweet below from 2019, you’ll see that I recommended buying Bitcoin at around $3,600. The same process that told me to buy Bitcoin back then is now telling me that we’ve probably seen the end of Bitcoin’s bull story.

Bitcoin had its chance. Since I recommended buying it in 2019, it has failed at pretty much everything besides appreciating in price. It never became a practical payment system. It failed the tests of inflation, Fed policy, money supply and being a store of value. It behaves like a risk asset, not the revolutionary currency we were promised.

You can invent patterns, call it a bear market, talk about cycles, but the only thing you’re really clinging to is hope.

I prefer to put my money where I see a better investment case. If Elon Musk is right about what SpaceX can accomplish, perhaps there’s an opportunity to make 5 to 10 times your money over the next decade.

Why spend another ten years hoping Bitcoin will finally do what you expected it to do five years ago?

I was bullish when the facts justified being bullish. The facts have changed, and so has my mind.

AI stocks doom & gloom: facts vs. fiction

The narrative is that the AI trade is cracking, valuations were absurd and a Dem-controlled Congress will throttle the data-centre buildout. Multiples have been crushed and sentiment is grim. Here's the separation of signal from noise.

Facts

Demand remains robust and supply-constrained. Nvidia's last reported quarter: revenue ~$96B (+106% YoY), data-centre ~$89B. Q3 guide ~$108B. Management has guided ~70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028 and explicitly called it supply-constrained (customer demand would support closer to a doubling). Bottlenecks (especially memory) are expected to persist into 2028. Omdia just raised its 2026 semiconductor forecast to +62.7%, driven by AI and a severe DRAM/NAND crunch. Hyperscaler capex is still climbing: big-4 2026 guidance is in the $700B+ range, with 2027 consensus estimates running $900B–$1.3T+ across the major players. Earnings estimates for the SOX have surged (rolling 12-month EPS estimates up ~155% this year in some measures); forward EPS for semis/AI infrastructure has been revised sharply higher even as prices fell.

Fiction / overreaction

This is not 1999–2000. Earnings and free cash flow are real and growing rapidly; the multiple compression is happening on rising estimates, not collapsing ones. The post-midterms selloff priced in a sharp, immediate halt to the buildout. Brokerages have called that reaction overdone (more likely some project delays into 2028–29) that could actually elongate the cycle and smooth supply/demand. Credit and ROI concerns are legitimate for the most leveraged names, but they do not erase the demand signals from the companies writing the cheques.

Where we are in the cycle

We are past the pure “narrative” phase and into a period of high growth with visible supply constraints and elevated (but still rising) hyperscaler spending. Some analysts flag a possible peak around 2027; others note that historical SOX bottoms have led fundamental turning points by 6–9 months. The SOX is already down ~38% from its June peak and trades at a multi-year low forward multiple. Changes in legislation will likely slow and elongate the capex cycle, not end it. 

Valuations

SOX forward P/E is now in the ~12–14x range (various sources cite ~10–13.7x; some as low as levels last seen in 2011/2019 or near the 2022 low). That is a ~20%+ discount to the S&P 500 and near historical cycle troughs. NDX forward P/E has compressed to the high teens / ~19x, in line with or below its longer-term median and the cheapest relative levels in years for the tech complex. These are attractive multiples relative to the growth rates still being guided and estimated, 

Conclusion

The depressed forward multiples on the SOX and NDX embed substantial skepticism about the duration of the AI capex cycle, political delays, credit conditions and the eventual ROI. They do not reflect a collapse in current demand or near-term guidance. If the demand trends and company commentary hold (supply tight, hyperscaler spend still rising, earnings revisions still positive), these levels look more like an opportunity - particularly in higher-quality, cash-flow-positive names - than a fully justified deep discount. Risks remain if spending rolls over earlier than expected or political friction proves more material. But the fundamentals have not yet broken; investor sentiment has. https://t.co/YKr5pL78cE

Some of the highest gross margin startups in SF right now aren’t SaaS companies. They’re basically data generation companies selling to AI labs.

I think every verifiable domain is going to get crushed by AI. Mathematics is the quintessential example. With Lean, you can formally prove whether a solution is correct. Software engineering is another one. You can run the code, run the tests, and know whether it works. Progress in these domains is insanely fast because you have a reliable reward signal.

But the next frontier is much harder. Think GDPval-style knowledge work, long-running workflows, complex tasks that take humans days or weeks to complete.

At the end of the day, models are only as good as the data and training environments we give them. And the labs need more and more high-quality reinforcement learning environments (RL envs) to keep scaling.

Physics, biology, healthcare, aerospace engineering, finance, you name it. Every domain needs its own environments, verifiers, simulations, and expert feedback.

So there’s almost unlimited demand for companies that can generate this data. And unlike SaaS companies building AI wrappers and paying for inference, these companies are selling the fuel for the next generation of models.

Extremely high margins, enormous demand, and we’re probably just getting started.

I came to the conclusion that most SaaS should become an MCP server.

we’re getting the economics of AI software backwards. A lot of AI startups are building their own chat interfaces, agents, and workflows, essentially reselling tokens from the big labs at low to negative gross margins. 

What if SaaS companies did the opposite?

Take HR software. Instead of building an AI assistant, become the best MCP server for HR. Expose tools to:

- Benchmark salaries against proprietary market data
- Run compensation reviews and calculate pay equity
- Model salary increases against a department’s budget
- Recommend promotions based on company policies
- Update employee compensation in the HRIS
- Manage approvals, permissions, and audit trails

Let ChatGPT, Claude, or Copilot handle the conversation, reasoning, and orchestration. Let the customer pay for the tokens.

The SaaS company keeps the valuable stuff: proprietary data, integrations, business logic, permissions, compliance, and the system of record.

You still charge a SaaS subscription, but you’re no longer paying to generate every answer. You can ship faster, with fewer engineers, and potentially restore software-like gross margins.

The next generation of SaaS might not have much of a UI at all. Just an incredibly good MCP server.

In some ways the new Fable is a monster. This is SimpleQA Verified from Epoch. There are few benchmarks like this where Fable 5.2 jaggedly jumped ahead of the entire pack.

For me there are two big indicators arriving next week that will tell us a lot about the shape of things going into 2027. I'm assuming two things happen next week: Anthropic releases their internal progress report (from which we will get updated numbers on RSI), and OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra.

With the new Astra, we will see how OpenAI answers Fable, and Fable needs to be answered. They need to close the gap, but they also need to close the gap that doesn’t show up on benchmarks: that a lot of people love working with the new Anthropic models, particularly Opus 5.5. And this is starting to tip the table a little.  Also expect another huge math release simultaneously with the new Astra. The previous one took five weeks and produced 700 papers; they've had another five weeks since then. They have also been working on other Millennium problems. Don't be shocked by anything. 

Astra's capability, and if it catches or surpasses Fable, is the first one. The second is where Anthropic is on AL4. The AI Futures Project (the AI 2027 guys) predict that AL4 reached 50% last month. If that's true, that means it will probably hit 80% by January. And at that point, assuming the overall pattern holds, some of the work at Anthropic will be at AL5 - aka fully autonomous with no human input. Probably about 5–10% of work at Anthropic would be at that level. If this number is actually higher than 50%, then things are moving even faster than believed, and that would be a big update for a lot of people, including me, who already has pretty short timelines. Above AL4 50% in October would probably mean RSI before the end of the year. Or possibly, already. So, a very important week for finding out where we are, and where we are headed.
